generation.title: Sequential compactness of images of closed subsets
generation.connection: Closedness keeps the subsequence limit in the chosen subset, so continuity sends it to a limit in that subset’s image.

ideas.title: Closed subsets
ideas.sourceQuote: A closed subset of a sequentially compact metric space is sequentially compact.

ideas.title: Continuous images
ideas.sourceQuote: The image of a sequentially compact metric space under a continuous map is sequentially compact.

assumptions: $K$ is a closed subset of $X$, equipped with the induced metric.

question.prompt: Constructed application of the two supplied source results: $X$ and $Y$ are metric spaces. $X$ is sequentially compact. $K$ is a closed subset of $X$, equipped with the induced metric. $f:X\to Y$ is continuous. Prove that $f(K)$, equipped with the metric induced from $Y$, is sequentially compact. Give a complete argument justifying the use of both closedness and continuity.
question.expectedAnswer: If $K=\varnothing$, then $f(K)=\varnothing$ and there are no sequences in $f(K)$, so sequential compactness holds vacuously. Otherwise, let $(y_n)_{n\geq 1}$ be any sequence in $f(K)$. For each $n$, choose $x_n\in K$ with $f(x_n)=y_n$. Since $(x_n)$ is a sequence in the sequentially compact space $X$, there are strictly increasing indices $n_j$ and a point $x\in X$ such that $x_{n_j}\to x$ in $X$. Closedness of $K$ in $X$ implies $x\in K$. Continuity of $f$ at $x$ gives $y_{n_j}=f(x_{n_j})\to f(x)$ in $Y$. Since $x\in K$, the limit $f(x)$ belongs to $f(K)$; convergence also holds in its induced metric. Thus every sequence in $f(K)$ has a subsequence converging to a point of $f(K)$, which proves the claim. This follows the two supplied source proofs in succession. A valid alternative is to justify that every sequence in $K$ has a subsequence converging in $X$ whose limit lies in $K$, thereby establishing sequential compactness of $K$, and then apply the supplied continuous-image theorem to the continuous restriction $f|_K:K\to Y$. The restriction is continuous because the metric on $K$ is induced from $X$.
gradingCriteria: Treat the empty case explicitly or through a valid vacuous universal argument, and start with an arbitrary sequence in $f(K)$ with preimages in $K$, or use the supplied continuous-image theorem on a justified domain.
Use sequential compactness of $X$ to obtain a subsequence of the chosen domain sequence converging to a point of $X$, either directly or when establishing sequential compactness of $K$.
Use closedness of $K$ in $X$ to place the domain subsequence limit in $K$, thereby justifying the required domain property.

Use continuity to obtain convergence of the corresponding image subsequence to a point of $f(K)$ and conclude sequential compactness; alternatively, justify continuity of the restriction and apply the supplied continuous-image theorem to the established sequentially compact domain.

refresher.sourceQuote: Closedness puts its limit in K.
refresher.explanation: The source’s closed-subset proof uses closedness to retain an existing limit: a sequence in a closed subset that converges in the ambient metric space has its limit in the subset. Closedness alone does not produce a convergent subsequence. This distinction is needed when returning to the original argument.

check.prompt: Let $C$ be a closed subset of a metric space $M$. Suppose $c_n\in C$ for every $n$ and $c_n\to c$ in $M$. Prove that $c\in C$.
check.expectedAnswer: Suppose $c\notin C$. Since $C$ is closed, $M\setminus C$ is open, so some ball $B_M(c,r)$ with $r>0$ lies in $M\setminus C$. Convergence implies that $c_n\in B_M(c,r)$ for all sufficiently large $n$, contradicting $c_n\in C$. Hence $c\in C$. No sequential compactness assumption is needed because convergence is already given.
